[...] Growth habit Chickpea develops a taproot and lateral roots to a depth of about 30 inches. The plant has an indeterminate growth habit which allows plants to develop new leaves after flowering has begun. Typically, chickpea growth and development is terminated by some form of environmental stress, such as drought or extreme heat. Late season rains can cause plants that appear to have gone dormant to resume development including flowering and seed set, complicating harvest management. Chemical [...] Climate Chickpea is a cool season crop that grows best when daytime temperatures are between 70 and 84 °F, and nighttime temperatures are between 64 and 70 °F. The crop does well in regions with 6-10 inches of growing season precipitation. Temperatures above 98 °F can cause stress during early flowering and pod development, resulting in reduced yields. results.description:
### Quick facts…

 Water stress during critical growth periods reduces yield and quality of crops.
 Crop water use (ET) at critical growth stages can be used in irrigation scheduling to avoid stressing crops.
 Crop water use (ET) is weather dependent as well as soil, water and plant dependent.
 Periodically check soil water at different depths within the root zone and at different growth stages to avoid stressing the crop during critical growth stages.

requirements.missing: No document identifies the specific chickpea growth stage most vulnerable to water deficit with quantified yield loss AND provides an irrigation timing recommendation. s5 quantifies yield loss (15–33 % of well-watered) and flower/pod abortion under terminal drought during the reproductive stage, but it withholds water entirely rather than prescribing irrigation timing. s0 and s2 note that flowering/pod set under heat and drought reduces yield, yet offer no stage-specific yield-loss figure or irrigation-schedule recommendation.

No document supplies measured soil-water inputs tied to the identified sensitive stage in the required units (kPa, %, mm, mm/day). s5 reports predawn leaf water potential in MPa and soil water content as % field capacity, but not in kPa or as volumetric water content, and provides no ETc, applied irrigation depth, or distinction between crop water use and applied water. s0 gives only a qualitative "2-3 inches per season" for irrigated vs. dryland yield difference without stage linkage or ETc.
